# Labeling Theory 

## How Did We Arrive Here? 

::: {.smaller-text}

<br>

Criminology began moving away from traditional explanations focused on:

<br>

Biology (e.g., Genetics)

Psychology (e.g., Psychopathology)

Social (e.g., Rational Choice Theory)

<br>

[Researchers started asking:]{.blue2}


[What if crime is shaped not just by the individual, but by how society reacts to them?]{.orange}

<br>

This period saw growing skepticism toward the [neutrality of police, courts, and other institutions]{.blue}

:::

## How Did We Arrive Here? 


::: {.smaller-text}

[What led to this growing skepticism?]{.blue2}

<br>

Civil Rights & Social Movements

Expanding juvenile justice systems and school discipline raised concerns about over-sanctioning youth

Scholars like Becker and Tannenbaum [argued that acts aren’t deviant - society makes them deviant through reactions]{.orange}

<br>

[Resulting Shift:]{.blue2}

Focus turned toward labels, stigma, identity, and power dynamics

Recognition that sanctions can produce unintended [criminogenic effects]{.blue}


:::


## Criminogenic Effects

::: {.small-text}

Refer to [social reactions, policies, or interventions that unintentionally increase the likelihood of future criminal behavior]{.blue}

<br>

In other words, an [iatrogenic effect]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} - [efforts meant to control crime can sometimes end up producing more crime]{.blue2}

<br>

Examples:

[School suspensions]{.violet} lead to more time with deviant peers

[Arrest records]{.violet} blocks people from employment and education (e.g., Pell Grants and FASFA access)

[Over-policing]{.violet} in minority communities leads to higher chance of criminalization and less trust

[Incarceration]{.violet} exposure to criminal networks 

:::


## Labeling Theory 



::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

:::{.smallest-text}

[Argues that deviance is not inherent in an act, instead deviance results from social reactions, definitions, and labels applied by others]{.blue2}

<br>

Once a label such as “delinquent,” “criminal,” “troublemaker” is applied, [it can shape a person's identity, opportunities, and future behavior via internalizing that label]{.blue}

<br>

[Important Elements:]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} 

1️⃣ No act is inherently deviant - behavior becomes deviant only when society defines it as such

2️⃣ “Deviant” labels are socially applied by parents, schools, police, courts, media, and peers

3️⃣ Social reactions can produce criminogenic effects

:::

:::


::: {.column width="50%"}



![](Images2/lab.png){.absolute top=130 right=40 height="70%"}

:::


:::


## Primary vs. Secondary Deviance

:::{.smaller-text}

[Primary Deviance:]{.blue}

Initial, [often minor rule-breaking]{.orange} (e.g., underage drinking) that typically doesn’t alter self-image

<br>

Example: A teen shoplifts once, isn’t caught, doesn’t adopt a “thief” identity

<br>

[Secondary Deviance:]{.blue} 

[Further deviance caused by society’s reaction and the internalization of a deviant label]{.orange}

<br>

Example: The teen is publicly labeled a “thief,” shunned, and then embraces that identity by committing more thefts

:::

## Dramatization of Evil 

::: {.small-text}

Coined by Frank Tannenbaum

[When society overreacts to minor misbehavior by defining the person - not the act - as “evil,” the individual becomes segregated and pushed into a deviant role]{.blue}

<br>

[This dramatization accelerates the transition from primary to secondary deviance]{.blue2}

<br>

Example:

1️⃣ A middle-school child cheats on one homework assignment 

2️⃣ Teachers begin referring to them as “a cheater,” and classmates avoid working with them

3️⃣ Feeling distrusted and discouraged, the student stops trying in class and cheats again

:::


## The Labeling Process

<br>

:::{.small-text}

1️⃣ [Initial Act (Primary Deviance):]{.blue} Usually minor, goes unnoticed or unpunished

<br>

2️⃣ [Detection & Labeling:]{.blue} Authorities or community apply a formal deviant label

<br>

3️⃣ [Stigmatization:]{.blue} Person faces social rejection; opportunities narrow

<br>

4️⃣ [Internalization:]{.blue} The label becomes part of self-identity, fueling continued deviance [(Secondary Deviance)]{.blue}

:::

::: notes

Self-Fulfilling Prophecy: Harsh labeling can deepen criminal behavior


:::



## Labeling as Criminogenic: Creating Career Criminals

::: {.smaller-text}

Labeling theory proposes that formal and informal societal reactions can push individuals into long-term criminal pathways, in other words - [career criminals]{.blue}

<br>

[Career criminals]{.blue} are [individuals who engage in persistent, long-term patterns of offending across their life course, often beginning with minor acts in childhood or adolescence and progressing into more serious or frequent criminal behavior over time]{.blue2}

<br>

[Mechanisms:]{style="text-decoration: underline;"}

Repeated labeling, surveillance, and exclusion lead to:

Reduce access to education, employment, and conventional peer groups

This process helps explain why some individuals become career criminals - not because of inherent traits, [but because social reactions intensify and prolong deviant identities]{.blue}


:::


## Criticisms of Labeling Theory

<br>

Overlooks [why]{.blue} deviance starts in the first place

<br>

Often used alongside other theories to fully explain criminal behavior

<br>

Difficult to test empirically

[Social Reaction Models]{.blue}

<br>

Refer to a broad group of criminological perspectives that explain crime and deviance as [products of social interaction and societal responses, rather than inherent qualities of the individual]{.blue2}

# Marxist Criminology 

## What is Marxism? 

:::{.small-text}

<br>

“A spectre is haunting Europe - the spectre of Communism.”

— Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848)

<br>

[Here](https://www.pbs.org/video/who-was-karl-marx-and-why-is-everyone-still-talking-about-him-yztklg/)

:::

## Karl Marx 


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::{.smallest-text}

Philosopher, economist, and social theorist (1818–1883)

<br>

Argued that society is shaped by [material conditions]{.violet}, especially how goods are produced and who controls that production

<br>

[Believed capitalism creates inequality, exploitation, and conflict, which undermine social solidarity]{.blue2}

<br>

Viewed the [state and the legal system as tools that protect the interests of the ruling class]{.orange}

<br>

[Saw crime as a symptom of the unequal social and economic structures produced by capitalism]{.blue}

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](Images2/marx.jpg){.absolute top=130 right=40 height="70%"}


:::

:::


## How Did We Get Here? 

:::{.smallest-text}

Marxist criminology trace back to the social and economic transformations of the 1800s, where [rapid social change]{.blue} created: 

<br>

1️⃣ Declining social cohesion 

2️⃣ Growing inequalities between *owners* and *workers*

3️⃣ Harsh labor conditions and lack of social mobility

4️⃣ Increase conflict between social classes (i.e., rich and poor)

<br>

Marx and Engels argued [that capitalism fundamentally reorganized society around competition, private property, and exploitation, creating an environment where social tensions were symptoms of structural problems]{.blue}

<br>

Believed the only solution was to find an alternative to Capitalism

<br>

Set the stage for [the development of Marxist perspectives on law, power, inequality, and ultimately crime]{.blue2}

:::

## Russian Revolution of 1917

:::{.smallest-text}

The Russian Revolution served as the historical flashpoint that transformed Marx and Engels’ ideas from theoretical critique into political reality

[It was driven by extreme economic inequalities between the bourgeoisie and proletariat, which produced widespread poverty, food shortages, and political repression]{.blue2}

[Bourgeoisie]{.blue} – the ruling class that owned the means of production

[Proletariat]{.blue} – the working class that sold their labor under exploitative conditions

<br>

1️⃣ [February Revolution]{.blue} – Mass protests and strikes forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate, ending centuries of imperial rule

2️⃣ [October Revolution]{.blue} – Led by the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin, this second uprising transferred power to the Soviets (worker councils), establishing the first major socialist state

<br>

A civil war then broke out between the Bolshevik Red Army and various anti-Bolshevik factions.

<br>

The Bolsheviks ultimately prevailed and, by 1922, created the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR).

:::



## Marxism

:::{.smallest-text}

Marxism is a theoretical framework developed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels to [explain how economic structures, power, and class relations shape social life]{.orange}

<br>

[Fundamental propositions:]{style="text-decoration: underline;"}

<br>

1️⃣ Conflict grows with inequality

*Differences in access to scarce resources intensify conflict between groups*

2️⃣ Those who receive less begin questioning the legitimacy of the system

*They recognize the structural “raw deal” and the exploitation shaping their conditions*

3️⃣ Oppressed groups eventually organize and bring conflict into the open

*This leads to polarization, social struggle, and attempts to redistribute resources*

4️⃣ Capitalism is the source of the conflict

*It generates extreme inequality, exploitation, and alienation*

<br>

This conflict-based understanding of society directly informs Marxist criminology

:::

## Marxist Criminology

:::{.smaller-text}

Examines how crime and law are shaped by economic structures and class power

<br>

[Core Ideas]{style="text-decoration: underline;"}

1️⃣ Crime is a symptom of capitalism

2️⃣ Inequality, poverty, and competition create criminogenic conditions

3️⃣ Human nature is innately social, capitalism distorts it into egoism and individualism

4️⃣ Both the poor and the powerful commit crime (but in different forms)

<br>

[Law & Power]{style="text-decoration: underline;"}

[Laws reflect the interests of the bourgeoisie or ruling class]{.blue}

[Behaviors threatening the bourgeoisie are more likely to be criminalized]{.blue}


:::

## Marxist Criminology

:::{.small-text}

*William Bonger*

<br>

Capitalism creates an “unfavorable environment” that increases both:

<br>

1️⃣ Crimes of survival (poverty)

2️⃣ Crimes of power (greed, exploitation)

<br>

Abolishing capitalism would restore social solidarity and reduce crime


:::
